question: How many arithmetic and comparison operations are necessary and sufficient to recall one of n memorized input-output pairs when a ReLU network may route each input through a different conditional computation path?

key_findings.claim: The paper gives a constructive dataset-level compiler whose per-example operation count scales with the active weights of a fitted ReLU network.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 builds a configuration tree from the zero/nonzero activation patterns induced by the training inputs. At each layer, the previously observed output configuration determines which next-layer neurons can receive a nonzero weighted input, so the conditional program computes only that restricted submatrix. For training input x_i with omega_i active weights, the stated bound is p+4 omega_i additions, multiplications, and comparisons while preserving its stored output d_i.

key_findings.claim: A balanced hyperplane-routing construction recalls n distinct fixed patterns with logarithmically many active switches when input and output dimensions are fixed.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 augments inputs with a constant, translates every coordinate positive, recursively splits each current finite subset in half with a hyperplane, and implements each split with a two-layer ReLU switch that sends the translated vector down one branch and zero down the other. A leaf-specific ReLU block writes the desired nonnegative output. Every memorized input traverses at most ceil(log_2 n) switches, yielding O(r+q log n) active neurons and O(rq+q^2 log n) active weights for q=p+1.

key_findings.claim: The comparison-tree converse is sound in spirit for the paper's exact-real, bias-free scalar-output model and generic-rank datasets.
key_findings.evidence: With at most alpha total operations, there can be at most alpha branching comparisons and thus at most 2^alpha leaves after also refining on ReLU signs. A fixed root-to-leaf path is a linear map in this model. If more than p samples reach one leaf, the assumed full rank of every stacked input-output block of p+1 samples contradicts one shared linear map. This gives alpha at least log_2(n/p), which becomes Omega(log n) only when p is fixed relative to n.

key_findings.claim: The headline Theta(log n) statement suppresses essential dependence on input and output dimensions.
key_findings.evidence: The actual achievability cost is O(rq+q^2 log n), q=p+1, rather than dimension-free O(log n). The converse is only log_2(n/p), can be constant or vacuous if p grows with n, and covers scalar outputs. The paper acknowledges after Theorem 3 that the bounds do not resolve dimension scaling. Abstract and conclusion state an unconditional Theta(log n) rate without the fixed-p, fixed-r qualification needed to match the results.

key_findings.claim: Low query computation is purchased with a much larger lookup structure, so the result is a compute-storage tradeoff rather than a capacity improvement at fixed model size.
key_findings.evidence: The conditional construction has a full binary tree with O(n) switches/nodes, width O(n), and depth O(log n); it stores a leaf block for every desired output. With fixed dimensions, only O(log n) of those units activate for one query, but all O(n) units and associated weights must exist. The cited unconditional construction uses roughly sqrt(n) polylogarithmic parameters. No theorem constrains total conditional parameters, bytes, build cost, or compute and storage jointly.

anchors.section: Appendix B, one leaf-specific output block per sample

key_findings.claim: The general synthesis theorem preserves only the enumerated dataset relationships, not the base network's function on unseen inputs.
key_findings.evidence: The configuration tree contains only output patterns observed while running the supplied finite dataset through the base network. Appendix A explicitly says an unseen input can reach a condition for which no output is defined and suggests merely reconnecting empty bins to make some output exist. Such reconnection does not prove equality to the unconditional network. Therefore claims that the compiler reproduces the same functionality or automatically converts a general sparse model are stronger than Theorem 1.

key_findings.claim: Even the direct memorizer's logarithmic bound holds only exactly on stored points and is not robust to nearby inputs.
key_findings.evidence: The switches use margins chosen from the finite set. The paper states that arbitrary inputs near decision hyperplanes can activate multiple branches and exceed the advertised active-neuron and active-weight bounds, though this region's Lebesgue measure can be shrunk by tuning weights. No separation radius, perturbation tolerance, Lipschitz bound, noisy-recall guarantee, or probability under an input distribution is supplied. An arbitrarily small-volume bad set can still contain every practically relevant perturbation around a stored point if margins are tiny.

key_findings.claim: The unit-cost real-arithmetic model hides parameter precision, memory access, and branch overhead that can dominate an actual memorizer.
key_findings.evidence: Every addition, multiplication by an arbitrary real weight, exact zero/equality test, and comparison costs one operation regardless of word length. Balanced separating hyperplanes and switch scales use gaps between projected data points and may need arbitrarily precise or large weights. The focal paper explicitly leaves bounded bit complexity to future work, whereas its own unconditional reference proves that large bit complexity is necessary for sublinear-parameter memorization. Weight fetches, cache misses, pointer traversal, and storing O(n) leaves are not counted.

key_findings.claim: The claimed advantage over unconditional neural memorization is not an advantage over ordinary indexed storage.
key_findings.evidence: The construction is structurally a balanced decision tree whose leaves store outputs; the paper itself calls it a classical binary decision tree. Comparison-based dictionaries already offer logarithmic lookup with linear storage, while finite-precision hashing can offer expected constant-time exact lookup under a different computational model. Learned indexes and product-key memories explicitly measure latency, bytes, and cache behavior. Thus the neural result is a representation theorem inside a chosen ReLU/comparison model, not an ultimate bound for memory recall in general.

key_findings.claim: The converse's generic-rank assumption does not cover many common classification memories.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 requires every subset of p+1 examples to make the vertically stacked input row block and scalar output row full rank p+1. The almost-sure justification samples both inputs and desired outputs independently from continuous positive-support distributions. Repeated discrete class labels can produce subsets with all-zero output or otherwise violate the condition, and vector-valued/one-hot outputs are outside the statement. The lower bound is therefore not a universal classification memorization lower bound.

key_findings.claim: The achievability and converse use different output and bias conventions.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 explicitly augments each input with a constant 1 to implement biases and requires every component of d_i to be nonnegative because the final operation is ReLU. Theorem 3 instead takes unaugmented x_i in R^p, scalar d_i in R, and relies on the fact that each fixed path is a homogeneous linear map. Allowing standard affine biases changes the number of points one affine leaf can fit and requires an adjusted rank condition. These differences are small for fixed p asymptotics but prevent a literal matching theorem under one identical model contract.

key_findings.claim: The paper suppresses logarithmic factors and overstates the scale of the unconditional-to-conditional improvement.
key_findings.evidence: The cited optimal unconditional construction actually uses O(sqrt(n) log n) weights/neurons, not plain O(sqrt(n)), and its optimality is only up to logarithmic factors. The conditional cost is O(q^2 log n+rq), not plain log n. Describing the change as almost exponential is an informal reparameterization of polynomial-versus-logarithmic query cost; the improvement ratio as a function of n is polynomial, and it is accompanied by growth from near-sqrt(n) to linear total storage.

key_findings.claim: The compiler proposal is not a trainable method for conditional generalization.
key_findings.evidence: To build the tree, one first trains an unconditional model, runs every stored sample through every layer, records exact zero/nonzero configurations, and materializes dataset-specific branches. The suggestion to regularize a base network so it is inactive and then place gates automatically is not accompanied by an optimization objective, generalization theorem, pruning baseline, or experiment. The author explicitly leaves effective training and generalization on practical datasets to future work.

key_findings.claim: The proof of Theorem 1 contains a repairable but explicit active-node versus active-weight counting error.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A defines a_l as the number of active nodes at layer l, then says their local fields require at most a_l multiplications and a_l additions. A dense active node can have many active incoming weights, so this statement is false with that definition. The intended proof works if a_l is redefined as the number of active weights: arithmetic then costs 2a_l and each active input-config neuron has at least one such weight, giving |IC_l|<=a_l. The printed derivation should not be accepted literally without this correction.

key_findings.claim: The printed converse has notation and asymptotic-label errors even though its fixed-dimension argument can be reconstructed.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 displays alpha>=log_2(n/p) as belonging to O(log n), whereas a lower-bound conclusion should be described with Omega after fixing p. In its proof, d_i is scalar but W_0 is called a q-by-p matrix although q is undefined there; it should be a one-by-p row map. These are visible in the rendered PDF and are not extraction artifacts.

key_findings.claim: No experiment verifies that operation counts translate into latency, energy, or useful predictive behavior.
key_findings.evidence: The paper contains theorem constructions and schematic figures only. It reports no implementation, dataset run, training success, wall-clock latency, batch throughput, branch divergence, parameter bytes, energy, or comparison with MoE, early exit, sparse kernels, search trees, or hash tables. The discussion acknowledges that aggressive conditioning conflicts with batching and that more work is needed, so empirical performance claims in the motivation are inherited from unrelated architectures rather than demonstrated by this construction.

key_findings.claim: The paper correctly separates memorization from generalization, but double descent does not bridge that gap for the proposed model.
key_findings.evidence: Section 1.3 explicitly says unseen-example generalization is a separate problem and outside scope. It cites double descent only to argue that memorization and generalization are not logically contradictory; this supplies no guarantee that the O(n)-leaf exact lookup tree generalizes, remains stable off the stored points, or can be learned by gradient descent. The construction's undefined and multi-path unseen behavior makes this distinction operationally important.

method.core_idea: Trade total model size for low per-query work by routing each memorized input through one logarithmic-depth path of a much wider ReLU decision tree, and prove a comparison-tree lower bound for generic exact-real memories.
method.mechanism: A dataset-specific compiler first records which neurons and nonzero weights activate for every training input and turns those activation configurations into if-else paths that calculate only active submatrices. For the direct upper bound, inputs are bias-augmented and translated positive; random projections plus a threshold split every finite subset approximately in half; two-layer ReLU switches copy a vector to one child and zero the other; recursion yields one leaf per sample; leaf-specific units emit nonnegative desired outputs and a final sum collects the lone active leaf. The converse expands all comparisons and ReLU signs into a binary computation tree and uses a rank condition to limit each linear leaf to p examples.
assumptions: The n input patterns are pairwise distinct and available when constructing the network.
Input and output dimensions are treated as constants when the result is summarized as Theta(log n).
Desired outputs in the constructive theorem have nonnegative components so a final ReLU can reproduce them.
Exact real additions, multiplications, and comparisons each cost one operation regardless of bit precision.
Total parameter storage, memory access, and branch dispatch are free in the theoretical operation count.
Exact zero/nonzero activation configurations can be detected reliably.
Performance is required only on the enumerated memorized inputs, not on surrounding or unseen inputs.
The converse uses scalar outputs and every p+1-example stacked input-output matrix has full rank.
Neural computations are homogeneous and bias-free in the converse; biases are represented only by explicitly augmented inputs in the construction.
A worst-case per-input operation budget, rather than total/average batch cost, is the relevant resource.

techniques.role: Compiles training-set zero/nonzero activation patterns into dataset-specific conditional paths.
Bounds compiled inference work by the number of nonzero connections relevant to one input.
Orders any finite distinct set along a generic projection and thresholds it into near-equal halves.
Uses two ReLU layers to copy a positive input to one branch and send zeros to the other on stored patterns.
Recursively isolates every stored example at a logarithmic-depth leaf.
Stores each desired output in weights attached to its unique leaf.
Counts at most 2^alpha computation leaves under alpha operations.
Rules out fitting p+1 generic scalar relationships with one homogeneous linear leaf map.
Adds a constant coordinate so the constructive ReLU network can translate data and store arbitrary nonnegative leaf outputs.
Counts only nodes and weights traversed by an exact member of the memorized dataset.

evaluations.setting: Arbitrary pairwise-distinct n-point dataset in R^p with nonnegative r-dimensional targets
evaluations.metric: Active neurons and active weights per exact stored input
evaluations.result: At most 2(q+1)ceil(log_2 n)+q+r active neurons and 12q(q+1)ceil(log_2 n)+(r+2)q+r-2 active weights, q=p+1
evaluations.baseline: Vardi-Yehudai-Shamir unconditional ReLU memorizer with roughly sqrt(n) polylogarithmic total and active parameters

evaluations.setting: Any fitted unconditional ReLU network evaluated on the finite dataset used to build its configuration tree
evaluations.metric: Compiled additions, multiplications, and comparisons on input x_i
evaluations.result: Theorem 1 states at most p+4 omega_i operations where omega_i is the input's active-weight count
evaluations.baseline: Naive execution of all weight-matrix entries in the base network

evaluations.setting: Scalar-output conditional networks on data satisfying every-subset generic rank
evaluations.metric: Worst-case operations alpha per memorized input
evaluations.result: Theorem 3 derives alpha at least log_2(n/p), giving logarithmic dependence only for fixed p

evaluations.setting: Practical inference, generalization, and hardware efficiency
evaluations.metric: Training success, held-out accuracy, latency, throughput, energy, memory, and branch efficiency
evaluations.baseline: No empirical MoE, early-exit, sparse-kernel, decision-tree, hash-table, or learned-index comparison

limitations: The Theta(log n) headline assumes fixed input and output dimensions; actual upper and lower bounds depend materially on p and r.
The construction uses O(n) nodes/leaves and unbounded total parameter storage to obtain logarithmic per-input work.
Theorem 1 preserves only the finite dataset relationships and can be undefined or differ from the base network on unseen inputs.
The direct memorizer's active-path bound holds only on exact stored patterns; nearby boundary inputs may activate multiple paths.
All real weights and exact comparisons have unit cost; bit complexity and numerical precision are ignored.
Memory access, cache behavior, branch dispatch, parallelism, batching, and communication are outside the operation model.
The achievability theorem requires nonnegative output components and explicitly augmented bias coordinates.
The converse has scalar outputs, no affine bias, and a strong every-subset rank assumption.
The generic-rank justification uses continuous random targets and does not cover many repeated discrete labels.
The printed Theorem 1 proof confuses active-node and active-weight counts, requiring a notation repair.
The printed converse labels its lower-bound expression with O(log n) and uses an undefined q for W_0.
Logarithmic factors in the unconditional reference and dimension factors in the conditional result are suppressed in the abstract.
The synthesis process can duplicate base-network computation across dataset configurations, but no total compiled-size bound is given.
No trainable objective realizes the proposed inactivity-to-gating compiler on practical data.
No empirical experiment, implementation, or artifact checks the construction, latency, energy, or generalization.
A standard balanced search tree already has the same linear-storage/logarithmic-query structure outside the neural formalism.
Generalization, noisy recall, approximate matching, updates/deletions, and distribution shift are all out of scope.
failure_modes: A slightly perturbed stored input crosses a separating hyperplane and reaches the wrong leaf.
A point inside a switch's narrow transition band activates more than one subtree and loses the logarithmic bound.
Finite-precision rounding changes an exact zero/nonzero activation configuration and selects an unbuilt branch.
Tiny projection gaps require very large switch scales, causing overflow or numerical instability.
An unseen activation configuration reaches a condition with no defined output in the compiled network.
O(n) randomly placed leaf parameters exceed cache or device memory, making sparse access slower than dense matrix multiplication.
A mini-batch routes to many leaves, destroying utilization through branch divergence and small per-branch batches.
Highly imbalanced real routing loads negate the balanced construction's depth and throughput assumptions.
Discrete labels violate the converse rank condition, so the advertised lower bound gives no information.
Growing p makes both the upper bound expensive and the lower bound weak or vacuous.
Negative regression targets cannot be emitted by the stated final ReLU construction.
A sparsity-trained base network has many activation configurations, causing the compiled tree to replicate a large fraction of the model.
Adding or modifying one stored pattern forces rebuilding hyperplane partitions and leaf parameters.
Exact memorization succeeds while every off-dataset prediction is meaningless, yielding no deployable learner.
reusable_insights: Always report conditional compute together with total parameters, parameter bytes, routing bytes, and build/training cost.
State which dimensions are fixed before compressing multivariate bounds into a single asymptotic rate in n.
Separate a function-preserving compiler from a finite-dataset lookup compiler; test equality on unseen inputs explicitly.
Conditional-operation lower bounds are only as general as their primitive operations, precision model, bias convention, and memory-access assumptions.
Active FLOPs do not predict latency without measuring batching, load balance, cache locality, dispatch, and sparse-kernel utilization.
A balanced tree is a useful constructive witness for conditional capacity, but classical dictionary and nearest-neighbor baselines reveal what is specifically neural.
For memorization theory, characterize a Pareto frontier over storage, query work, bit complexity, robustness radius, and update time rather than query arithmetic alone.
Use finite margins and quantized weights if a construction is intended to survive numerical implementation.
Report intention on discrete labels and vector outputs rather than using a continuous-target generic-rank condition as a universal proxy.
Test exact stored points, noisy variants, interpolations, unseen points, and adversarial boundary points separately.
Compiler claims should include total compiled graph size and worst-case unseen configuration growth.
Mechanically check proof notation where active nodes and active edges lead to different arithmetic counts.
open_questions: What is the optimal joint tradeoff among total weights S, per-query operations T, dimension p, output dimension r, and bit precision for ReLU memorization?
Can one achieve logarithmic query work with near-sqrt(n) rather than linear total parameters?
Can a compiler preserve a fitted network's function on an entire input domain rather than only a finite dataset?
How does a required perturbation margin or Lipschitz/noisy-recall guarantee change the storage-query lower bound?
What lower bound holds for standard affine ReLU networks with one-hot or repeated discrete labels?
Can a differentiable routing objective learn a balanced logarithmic tree while preserving useful generalization?
How do hash routing, product-key lookup, approximate nearest neighbors, and learned indexes compare under one memory/latency/energy budget?
What is the batch-average or distribution-weighted analogue of the paper's worst-case per-input operation bound?
Can routing paths be laid out and reordered to preserve GPU/TPU utilization and cache locality at O(n) scale?
How efficiently can the memory be updated online without rebuilding the full partition tree?
Can finite-precision switch margins be optimized to minimize both wrong routing and extra active paths?
Does conditional memorization capacity predict factual recall or interference in modern sparse language models once generalization and approximate matching are included?

competitive_landscape.title: On the Optimal Memorization Power of ReLU Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Vardi, Yehudai, and Shamir construct ReLU networks with roughly sqrt(N) parameters, prove near-optimality via VC dimension, characterize depth tradeoffs, and show that large bit complexity is necessary for sublinear parameters. The focal paper trades that compact storage for an O(N)-node routing tree and omits precisely the bit-complexity axis highlighted by its baseline.

competitive_landscape.title: Provable Memorization via Deep Neural Networks using Sub-linear Parameters
competitive_landscape.difference: Park et al. use depth to memorize N separated pairs with O(N^(2/3)) parameters and include empirical support. The focal method improves active query work with hard routing but expands total storage to linear and provides no experiment, making the two methods complementary points on an unmeasured size-compute frontier.

competitive_landscape.title: Small ReLU networks are powerful memorizers: a tight analysis of memorization capacity
competitive_landscape.difference: Yun, Sra, and Jadbabaie prove tight sqrt(N) width for three-layer networks under their setting, extend finite-sample expressivity through depth, and study SGD near a memorizing solution. The focal paper counts input-conditional operations instead of width and does not address whether its tree can be found by gradient training.

competitive_landscape.title: Memory capacity of neural networks with threshold and ReLU activations
competitive_landscape.difference: Vershynin gives probabilistic sparse constructions for threshold and mixed threshold/ReLU networks. The focal compiler is motivated by exploiting inactive weights, but it does not compare total sparsity, precision, or execution against this established sparse-capacity line.

competitive_landscape.title: Memorization capacity of deep ReLU neural networks characterized by width and depth
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang and Yang explicitly characterize a width-depth product under a separation distance delta and discrete labels, supplying matching upper/lower scaling in that regime. It sharpens two gaps in the focal analysis: robustness/separation is a first-class parameter and discrete labels are covered rather than justified through continuously random outputs.

competitive_landscape.title: Conditional Computation in Neural Networks for faster models
competitive_landscape.difference: Bengio et al. use policy gradients to learn activation-dependent block dropout against an accuracy-compute objective and report empirical speed improvements. The focal paper replaces learned routing with a dataset-specific exact compiler, obtaining a clean bound but no generalization or systems evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
competitive_landscape.difference: Sparsely gated MoE demonstrates a practical capacity-compute tradeoff at up to 137 billion parameters with trainable top-k routing and distributed language tasks. The focal theorem explains how conditional paths can decouple total and active capacity, but its unit-cost lookup tree does not model gate training, load balance, communication, or prediction quality.

competitive_landscape.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
competitive_landscape.difference: Switch routing activates one expert per token and measures pretraining speed, communication, stability, low-precision behavior, and multilingual quality. It shows why elementary operation counts are incomplete: practical sparse gains require explicit load, dispatch, and hardware engineering absent from the focal analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Hash Layers For Large Sparse Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Hash layers deterministically select token-specific weights without learned gates, load-balancing losses, or assignment algorithms and match or beat learned MoE variants empirically. They provide a direct practical alternative to the focal paper's claim that activation configurations must be compiled into a branching tree.

competitive_landscape.title: Large Memory Layers with Product Keys
competitive_landscape.difference: Product-key memory indexes up to a billion learned values with fast exact nearest-neighbor selection and reports accuracy and twofold inference speed gains. It tackles the same large-storage/small-active-compute goal while supporting approximate semantic lookup, not merely exact equality on stored real vectors.

competitive_landscape.title: Memorizing Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Memorizing Transformers perform approximate k-nearest-neighbor lookup over non-differentiable key-value memories and show scaling gains through 262K tokens across text, code, mathematics, and theorem data. The focal work provides exact finite-pattern theory but no mechanism for approximate contextual keys or evidence that memorized relations improve a task.

competitive_landscape.title: Fast Feedforward Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Fast Feedforward Networks use hard binary routing to select logarithmically many nodes from an exponentially large leaf set and report up to 220x feedforward and 6x MoE speedups. This is the closest practical successor to the focal tree idea: it trains on real tasks and measures latency, though it does not provide the same exact memorization lower bound.

competitive_landscape.title: The Case for Learned Index Structures
competitive_landscape.difference: Learned indexes treat lookup as predicting record position and compare neural models with cache-optimized B-trees in both memory and wall-clock speed. They expose the missing systems baseline for a construction that is functionally a dataset-specific index but counts neither stored bytes nor cache behavior.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper establishes an almost exponential advantage for conditional ReLU computation: n arbitrary input-output relationships can be recalled in Theta(log n) operations per input rather than roughly sqrt(n), and any fitted sparse network can be compiled into a computationally efficient conditional one.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The balanced switch construction is a substantive exact upper bound on stored nonnegative relationships, and the comparison-tree/rank argument supplies a matching fixed-dimension lower bound within a narrow exact-real model. The activation-configuration compiler is also an interesting dataset-level connection between unstructured ReLU sparsity and explicit routing.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The novel core is best described as a neural restatement and analysis of the linear-storage/logarithmic-query decision-tree tradeoff, plus a finite-dataset activation-pattern compiler. It is not a dimension-free or storage-free conditional capacity theorem: the upper bound is O(q^2 log n+rq), the lower bound is log(n/p) for scalar generic-rank data, total size is O(n), precision is unbounded, off-dataset behavior is not preserved, and no practical training or hardware result is supplied. Prior memorization theory provides compact sqrt(n)-scale storage; prior MoE, hash, and product-key work already realizes large inactive capacity; and later Fast Feedforward Networks directly trains and times a log-routing architecture. The theoretical construction is useful, but the abstract's almost-exponential and ultimate-limit framing omits the central storage, dimension, precision, robustness, and systems qualifications.

reviewer_notes: Read all 19 pages of the exact primary arXiv version, including every theorem, proof, algorithm, figure, footnote, and discussion. Rendered and visually inspected all PDF pages because the extractor warned about rotated text; specifically verified Theorem 3's log_2(n/p) expression, its O(log n) label, the W_0 dimension typo, Figures 1-6, and the Appendix A active-node counting paragraph. Researched and revision-checked current primary arXiv competitors through 2026-08-23 across ReLU memorization bounds, bit complexity, conditional computation, sparse MoE and hashing, structured/external memory, learned indexes, later log-time feedforward routing, and 2026 width-depth-separation theory.
